newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH CROWN JUMPS, THEN WAITS ON WED TRADE RESULTS.
newsitem.headline: CZECH CROWN JUMPS, THEN WAITS ON WED TRADE RESULTS.

text.p: The Czech crown on Tuesday recovered some of its losses of recent days, but dealers said one large trade caught the Prague market off guard, and firmed the currency ahead of Wednesday's foreign trade figures.

Mid-afternoon the crown was at 26.816 to the dollar, 17.713 to the mark or 3.02 percent above the central bank's weighted mark/dollar basket, mainly on the strength of a large purchase, but then eased toward the central bank fixing of +2.80 percent.

"There was a huge Czech crown purchase coming through the whole morning from outside the Czech Republic, and this caused a lot of the participants on the market to be short (in crowns)," said Petr Korous at CSOB in Prague.
"This was a totally contrarian move," Korous added, saying it was not yet clear who was behind the large trade.
The crown opened the morning just barely higher than two percent above parity of the mark/dollar basket, after the central bank's fixing at +2.61 percent on Monday.

Korous said the sentiment on the market was still mostly negative as the government gets battered by the opposition about recent problems of Czech banks, repeatedly calling for the dismissal of Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik.
The crown had been dropping since the middle of last week when it traded more than four percent above the basket.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and his Civic Democratic Party have refused to recall Kocarnik, and have primarily blamed the Czech National Bank for lax supervision in the failure of Kreditni Banka a.s. and illiquidity at Agrobanka a.s..

But dealers said they expected crown buying to remain cautious in the afternoon, as the market awaits the latest update on the steadily widening trade deficit when August merchandise results are released on Wednesday morning.
Oto Otepka at Girocredit said the market would react negatively if Wednesday's results implied a foreign trade deficit that might surpass 150 billion to 160 billion crowns for the entire year.
"If the projection of August figures exceeds this range then the markets will get very cautious and probably sell Czech crowns," Otepka said.
The record July deficit of 16.4 billion crowns put the seven-month trade gap at 85.3 billion crowns.

If the deficit rose an averge of 16 billion crowns per month for the remaining four months, the full-year 1996 deficit would come in at just under 150 billion crowns, estimated at between five to six percent of gross domestic product.
